name: Parapara dance

lead: Para Para is a Japanese group dance where each song has its own fixed routine, mostly arm and upper-body motion in time with Eurobeat or Eurodance. It grew in Japanese discos and was embraced by gyaru fashion culture.

For looks, its role is mainly as part of a styled scene: dancers coordinate outfits, makeup and hair, and the routine is a social activity within that look. Any physique benefit would come from the activity itself, which has not been studied for Para Para.

paras: Dancers learn song-specific routines from classes, club events, videos and online tutorials, then perform them in sync as a group. Many pair it with gyaru styling. Learning moves online and through fan convention panels is common outside Japan.
Low-intensity dance with the usual risks of club or convention settings. No specific harms are documented.

chain: Fits the gyaru aesthetic and social scene
angle.text: Para Para is a social, style-linked activity. It supports the gyaru look as part of a shared scene; no direct effect on physical appearance has been studied.

lead: Para Para (パラパラ) is a synchronised dance from Japan in which each song has its own choreography, similar to line dancing [1]. It is mostly upper-body and arm work with side-to-side steps over a four-on-the-floor beat, and is strongly tied to Eurobeat and Eurodance [1].

Gyaru culture amplified its early popularity [1]. In appearance terms, the dance sits inside a styled subculture in which clothes, hair and makeup are part of the performance; people take part for the look and social scene as much as for fitness.

paras: Wikipedia gives two theories of origin: men choreographing dances in club VIP rooms in the early 1980s to impress patrons, or the Takenoko-zoku dancers in Harajuku's Yoyogi Park [1]. A first boom (1987-92) took place in upscale bubble-era discos, a second (1993-95) produced many routines still used, and Avex released the VHS ParaPara Kyoten 0 in March 1994 [1].

A third boom (1999-2001) was partly driven by television after Takuya Kimura of SMAP performed a routine [1]. The 2006 drama Gal Circle and the manga Gals! featured it [1]. A fourth boom (2005-10) included anime-song routines, after which the scene declined and moved online [1]. Konami's Para Para Paradise arcade game used motion sensors for arm movements [1].
